newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries seen holding positive tone on Monday.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries seen holding positive tone on Monday.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries prices were expected to maintain a positive tone throughout the remainder of the trading session on Monday as investors awaited consumer price data on Tuesday.

Players' optimism was buoyed by a 0.3 percent fall in producer prices last week as well as weaker-than-expected retail sales data. Economists said the data seen last week could be convincing enough to keep the Federal Reserve's policy-making arm from further tightening at its July meeting. Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has made it clear he wanted to see a slowdown in the economy before refraining from further tightening of policy.
Jerry Zukowski, economist at PaineWebber Inc., said the firm tone seen throughout morning trading likely would hold up before the release of CPI data on Tuesday.
He said economic numbers remained favorable to the bond market, but another rally was unlikely following last week's gains. "I don't know if they'll (Tuesday's data) be supportive enough," he said.
Besides consumer prices, industrial production and capacity utilization, housing starts, real earnings and the Redbook and BTM/Schroders were scheduled for release.
"CPI looks to be benign. It would probably take some technical factors to move the market," Zukowski said.
Due for realease at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT was the National Association of Home Builders survey, which Zukowski doubted would have much market impact.
The market was mostly marking time on Monday, awaiting Tuesday's data, said Stuart Hoffman, senior economist at PNC Financial Corp.
"The market expects the numbers to be favorable with low inflation and a drop in new housing starts," Hoffman said.

Barring an unpleasant surprise in CPI, the bond market likely would hold on to gains seen in the past couple of weeks, Hoffman said. However, economic growth was not nearly as strong as the pace seen in the first quarter, he added.
"There was a little buying tied to passive portfolio managers needing to rebalance," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.
Strauss said yields were not currently attractive, but portfolios managers were forced to invest.
He warned that consumers had the ammunition to put money back into the markets despite the slowdown seen second quarter growth.
The Treasury's 30-year issue was up 10/32 yielding 6.70 percent.
Three-month bill rates were one basis point lower at 4.83 percent. Six-month bill rates were also down one basis point at 5.11 percent as well as year bills at 5.32 percent.
Five-year notes were priced at 100-30/32, up 3/32 to yield 6.28 percent. Ten-year notes were trading at 101-20/32, up 7/32, to yield 6.40 percent.
